transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for calling S-Net technical support, my name is Umar. How can I help you today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hi Umar. I run a commercial wedding photography business from home on your Gigafast 900 package, but our upload speed has collapsed to less than ten megabits today. I have four hundred gigabytes of raw 4K wedding footage to upload to our cloud archive before our client deadline tonight, and at this rate it's going to take four days!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I understand how critical fast upload speeds are when you have 400 gigabytes of client wedding footage to deliver ahead of tonight's deadline, Abigail. Let me investigate your optical uplink and bandwidth profiles immediately.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you Umar, because my clients are expecting their preview gallery tonight.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Before we run diagnostics on your optical link, Abigail, could you please verify your installation address and your four-digit account security PIN?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, it is 52 St Martin's Lane, York, YO1 6LN, the PIN is 3925, and my Synology NAS backup drive is hardwired into LAN port two of the Hub using a Cat6 Ethernet cable with a fifty-megabit bandwidth limit set in the backup software.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for verifying those details and providing that setup context, Abigail. I have your full fibre optical circuit open on our central telemetry console.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Great, thanks for getting into the account so quickly.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So just to confirm what you are experiencing: you subscribe to our Gigafast 900 symmetrical package with expected nine hundred megabit upload speeds, but your upstream throughput has dropped to under ten megabits today, severely delaying an urgent four-hundred-gigabyte client video delivery. Is that correct?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, exactly. Downstream speed is flying at nine hundred and twenty megabits, but upstream is crawling at seven to nine megabits.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: When download throughput is at nine hundred megabits while upload throttles below ten, it indicates either an upstream optical framing buffer misconfiguration or local interface port negotiation errors.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Could it be a problem with the optical fiber cable outside?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Checking our optical power levels at the York central optical line terminal... your received optical power is minus eighteen dBm and your transmit optical power is plus two dBm, which are well within optimal optical margins.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So the physical fiber light signal is healthy?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, the physical optical line is completely clean with zero bit error rate.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What else could be throttling the upload speed?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let me examine the upstream traffic policing profile applied to your optical network terminal.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What does the traffic policing profile do?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Our dynamic provisioning system assigns Quality of Service upstream rate shapers based on current tariff subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Did the rate shaper get set to the wrong tier?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Looking at your ONT configuration logs... during an automated firmware update last night, the upstream traffic shaper defaulted to our legacy broadband profile of ten megabits instead of symmetrical gigabit.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So your system update accidentally capped our upload speed to ten megabits!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, the automated firmware provisioning script failed to restore the symmetrical profile tag after the reboot.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Can you push the symmetrical gigabit profile back down to the ONT remotely?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, I can re-provision the symmetrical optical service profile directly from our engineering management terminal.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: How long does that re-provisioning take to apply?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The new bandwidth profile pushes down to your ONT and flashes into the hardware memory within about two minutes.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is fantastic news if that restores our nine hundred megabits upload.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Please bear with me while I place you on a brief hold for about two minutes while I push the symmetrical gigabit profile to your ONT.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for your patience while holding, Abigail. The symmetrical 900Mbps profile has been re-applied to your ONT.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you Umar. Should I run a speed test now from my computer?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let's first verify the local Ethernet link speed between your computer and the Hub.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Checking network adapter status in Windows... it says link speed is one thousand megabits full duplex.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Now open the Ookla Speedtest app and initiate a test against the S-Net Manchester server.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Starting speed test... download is nine hundred and thirty megabits... and upload shot straight up to eight hundred and eighty-five megabits!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Eight hundred and eighty-five megabits confirms full symmetrical bandwidth has been restored across your optical circuit.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That is incredible! At eight hundred and eighty-five megabits, my four hundred gigabytes of wedding footage will finish uploading in about an hour!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That will give you plenty of time ahead of tonight's client delivery deadline.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You have saved my business from a massive client complaint today.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Now, just so I can document the hardware setup on the support ticket, which LAN port on the Hub is your backup drive connected to again, and what category of Ethernet cable are you using?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's plugged into LAN port two with a Cat6 cable, exactly like I told you when we started the call.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you, Abigail. I have updated the hardware ticket notes.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: And what about the fifty-megabit limit in the software? Should I turn that off?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, in your Synology backup manager, set upload bandwidth to unlimited so it utilizes your full eight hundred and eighty-five megabits.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Changing bandwidth limit to unlimited now... the live upload graph in Synology just jumped to one hundred and ten megabytes per second!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: One hundred and ten megabytes per second represents maximum gigabit network saturation.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The progress bar says estimated time remaining is forty-eight minutes.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I have locked that symmetrical profile tag on your account so future firmware updates cannot overwrite it.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That proactive locking is very reassuring.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Does the Hub router prioritize NAS backup traffic over general household Wi-Fi?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The Hub 5 uses dynamic flow queuing to balance high-throughput wired traffic with latency-sensitive wireless streaming.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So my partner can still watch 4K television downstairs while the backup uploads?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, television streaming packets are tagged with high DSCP priority so they experience zero stuttering.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That prevents any household friction while my huge upload completes.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What happens to the cloud upload if our household electricity cuts out briefly during the transfer?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Synology Hyper Backup features block-level resumable uploads, so it resumes transferring the exact chunk where it left off.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That saves having to re-upload the entire four hundred gigabytes from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The checksum manifest verifies data integrity block by block upon resumption.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That gives me total technical confidence in our studio backup pipeline.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: We also recommend enabling email digest alerts on your Synology NAS upon successful task completion.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'll enable email digests so I get a notification once all four hundred gigabytes finish.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Alright, I've got another technical call waiting in queue. Goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Wait, Umar, don't you need to give me a reference number?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: The ticket is saved. Thank you for choosing S-Net today, Abigail. Have a good afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thanks Umar, goodbye.
